title: Re'eh: rejoice together (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14)
hookLine: rejoice at the festival with the servant, the stranger, the orphan and the widow

cards: A really good wedding. The music, the dancing, the food. Now look at who's there.
Family, old friends, coworkers. Who isn't? The neighbor who lives alone.
The new guy at work who doesn't know anyone yet. Nobody left them out on purpose. They just weren't on the list.

A celebration tends to draw its circle around the people already loved. The Torah's festival law draws that circle, then keeps going, naming people one by one until the guest list looks very different.

teach.h: THREE FESTIVALS, AND A COMMAND TO REJOICE.
teach.b: Deuteronomy sixteen walks through the three pilgrimage festivals: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. For Shavuot and Sukkot, it commands joy. In the old Jewish translation, of Sukkot: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast."
The Hebrew word for that joy is today's word, simcha. Then the guest list.

Thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy servants, and the Levite, who, Deuteronomy says elsewhere, has no portion of land, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates.
Rashi, the medieval commentator, counts them in two groups of four.

teach.h: FOUR OF YOURS, FOUR OF MINE.
teach.b: Four are yours: son, daughter, manservant, maidservant. Four are God's: the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. And he imagines God saying: if you make Mine happy, I'll make yours happy.
Maimonides, in a line from earlier this year, makes it sharper.
In his law code he writes that someone who locks his courtyard gates and eats and drinks with his family, but doesn't feed the poor and the grieving, isn't having the joy of a commandment at all.
He's having the joy of his stomach.

teach.h: WHO ELSE IS AT THE TABLE?
teach.b: So in Jewish law, simcha isn't only a feeling.
It's something you make, and you can't fully make it alone, or only with your own. Joy, in this chapter, is measured partly by who else is at the table.

how: Jewish law treats joy on the festivals, especially Sukkot, as a commandment, and some families make a point of inviting guests, newcomers and people who would otherwise be alone to holiday meals.

o: a wedding feast held on the night of a festival
joy, the festival kind, made bigger by sharing it
the pilgrimage up to the Temple three times a year

games.q: inside the guest list — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah commands joy at the festivals
"And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast."
Maimonides says a family feast behind locked gates fulfills the joy of the festival
without feeding the poor and grieving, he calls it the joy of his stomach.
the Levite is on the guest list because he has no land of his own
along with the stranger, the orphan and the widow.

games.q: you're planning a festival meal. according to Deuteronomy, who's on the list?
o: your family, your workers, and the Levite, stranger, orphan and widow.
games.why: Rashi counts four of yours and four of God's, and imagines God saying: make Mine happy, and I'll make yours happy.

practice: Five hundred days of this is worth a small celebration, and it's yours.

Now picture the next gathering in your life, a birthday, a holiday meal, a Sabbath dinner, even coffee, and set Rashi's other four beside the table: the stranger, the one alone, the one grieving, the one without people nearby.
Let one face come, and picture the seat beside you with them in it.

wordCard.voice: Simcha. Joy, the festival kind, commanded in Deuteronomy and made bigger by who you bring in.

orig.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness. in Deuteronomy, the joy the festivals command.

carryVoice: Your line: rejoice together. Five hundred days, and the table just got bigger. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast
